venue.name: Cowichan Valley Museum and Archives
venue.description: A community museum in the middle of Duncan, run by the Cowichan Historical Society, a non profit founded in 1974. It is housed in the 1912 E&N Duncan train station in Charles Hoey V.C. Memorial Park, surrounded by totem poles and gardens. Displays cover the valley from Duncan's beginnings as Duncan's Crossing in 1886, and include a re-creation of the Alderlea general store and the Jack Fleetwood Gallery. Admission to the museum is by donation, and the museum publishes two booked programs for school classes at $60 a class. The archives are on the third floor of Duncan City Hall on Craig Street and are open by appointment only.

programs.name: Museum tour with scavenger hunt
programs.description: A visit to the museum for a class, either led by a guide or run by the teacher. Children work through a scavenger hunt to find artifacts, photographs and information in each gallery, and the museum provides the clipboards and the hunt sheets. The museum lists it for Kindergarten to Grade 12 at 60 minutes, or a length of your choosing, for $60 a class. It is available from 15 September to 15 December and 15 January to 15 June, Monday to Wednesday, morning or afternoon. You arrange it by email.
programs.what_children_do: Walk the galleries with a clipboard, hunting for particular artifacts, photographs and pieces of information in each room, either following a guide or working through the hunt on their own.
programs.our_note: The $60 is for the whole class, not for each child, which makes this one of the cheaper indoor outings in the valley. They will run it for any length you ask for, so say up front how long your group can hold attention rather than taking the 60 minutes as fixed.
programs.practical_summary: Food and drink are not allowed inside, and the museum sits in Charles Hoey V.C. Memorial Park, which is where a packed lunch would have to happen. There is a free three hour car park just north of the train station and two hour free street parking on Duncan Street behind the museum, but nothing about coach parking, toilets or step free access is published.

programs.name: Duncan's Chinatown tour at the museum
programs.description: A 90 minute session at the museum for Grades 4 to 6, costing $60 a class. It covers what brought Chinese people to Canada and the Cowichan Valley, the discrimination and difficulties they faced, the people who made a difference, and the eventual demolition of Duncan's Chinatown. Children look at Chinese mementos based on artifacts in the museum's collection. The site says the tour is at the museum, not out on the street. You arrange it by email.
programs.what_children_do: Sit and move through the museum with a guide, looking at Chinese mementos based on objects in the collection and hearing how Duncan's Chinatown grew, who lived there and how it came to be pulled down.
programs.our_note: This one is pitched at Grades 4 to 6 and the subject includes discrimination, so it lands better with a class that has already talked about it. It is half an hour longer than the general museum tour for the same price, so ask whether the two can be combined into one morning.
programs.practical_summary: It all happens indoors at the museum, so weather is not a problem. There is nowhere inside to eat, and toilets, step free access and coach parking are not mentioned on the site.

Coach or bus parking: not mentioned. The site describes a free three hour car park just north of the train station and two hour free street parking on Duncan Street behind the museum, but says nothing about where a bus would go.
Which months and days the Chinatown tour runs: the site gives dates and days only for the general museum tour, so we left them blank for the Chinatown one. Months for the Chinatown tour are unknown.
Whether the $60 class fee is instead of the by donation admission or on top of it: not stated.
Whether the museum takes daycare or preschool groups: not addressed. Both published programs are written for school grades.
The site publishes no coordinates and its map on the contact page is drawn by script with no latitude or longitude in the page, so the pin still has to be filled in from the street address.

The site's main social sharing photograph is an archive image of the Canadian Scottish Regiment departing, not a picture of the museum as it is now, so we used the museum interior photograph from the tours page as the main picture instead. There is no exterior photograph of the train station anywhere on the site.
